blocks.text: Nahum’s portrayal of Nineveh under attack can be read alongside a Babylonian Chronicle that records Babylonian and Median campaigns culminating in the city’s capture and destruction in 612 BCE. Assyrian inscriptions and palace reliefs also illuminate an imperial world that presented conquest, tribute, violence, deportation, and lion symbolism in royal terms; such materials are royal representations, not neutral reports.

The identity of the “dasher in pieces” in verse 1 is not certain, though it probably refers to forces advancing against Nineveh. Verses 1–10 move rapidly through preparations, flashing chariots, a breached gateway, collapse, flight, and plunder, creating the sensory force of a siege poem. The river gates, palace, and pool imagery may be read in light of Nineveh’s hydraulic setting, but the passage does not establish that a literal flood caused the breach. The lion den in verses 11–13 turns Assyrian royal lion imagery into a taunt: the once-feared den is emptied, before the chapter ends with the LORD’s declaration against Nineveh. Later, Pesher Nahum reused Nahum’s words for Second Temple political and sectarian figures, showing that the chapter was also reread in a new setting.
